questions.stem: A 75-year-old man presented with fever, sepsis, and a painful left cheek. He had a history of diabetes treated with metformin. He had an ultrasound that revealed no abscess in the parotid. He was started on broad treatment with vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam along with volume resuscitation and was admitted to the ICU.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus S. aureus is the most common cause of suppurative parotitis. Diabetic and elderly patients are at higher risk for developing parotitis. An antistaphylococcal agent would be indicated as empiric coverage.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q10

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis underwent bilateral lung transplant under alemtuzumab induction. The patient was known to be colonized with Aspergillus fumigatus preoperatively and received posttransplant antifungal prophylaxis with voriconazole. Her immediate postoperative course was complicated by acute kidney injury requiring hemodialysis. On postoperative day 18, the nurse noted a 4×6 cm left buttock decubitus wound with a black eschar. There was no surrounding erythema. Excisional debridement was performed. The underlying gluteus muscle was necrotic and liquefied. An organism grew on Sabouraud agar after 4 days of incubation. Microscopy demonstrated broad hyphae without septa. Rootlike hyphae were also noted.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Decrease immunosuppression and perform serial wound debridements
Measure serum voriconazole concentration and adjust the antifungal dose accordingly

questions.explanation: Switch to liposomal amphotericin B The microscopic finding of nonseptate hyphae is consistent with an agent of mucormycosis. Rhizoids (rootlike hyphae) are typically produced by Rhizopus spp. Voriconazole has no activity against Rhizopus. Breakthrough infections while on voriconazole prophylaxis have been reported. Renal failure requiring hemodialysis is a risk factor for the disease. Hospital outbreaks have been associated with the use of contaminated linen which may have been the source in this case. Amphotericin B in combination with adequate surgical debridement is the treatment of choice. Treatment can be stepped down to posaconazole or isavuconazole after clinical improvement. However, initial therapy with an azole as a single agent is not recommended. Lomentospora prolificans (formerly Scedosporium prolificans ) is inherently resistant to all antifungals. Lomentospora forms septate hyphae with branching similar to Aspergillus spp.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q29

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman was reviewed with a 3-week history of fevers and a 1-week history of painful skin nodules. She was known to have a persistent neutropenia following an allogeneic stem cell transplant 4 weeks earlier for relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. She had been taking levofloxacin, voriconazole, valaciclovir, and trimethoprim– sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis; the levofloxacin had been switched to intravenous cefepime 3 weeks earlier, but her symptoms had progressed. On examination, her temperature was 103°F (39.4°C), her blood pressure was 110/68 mmHg, her heart rate was 116 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturations 98% on room air. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams were unremarkable. There were multiple subcutaneous purplish popular and nodular lesions of various sizes scattered throughout her extremities, her neck, and her chest. Some of the lesions had central necrosis. She had pedal onychomycosis. Investigations: Total white cell count 0.2 ×109 /L (4–10) Absolute neutrophil count 0.0 ×109 /L (2–8) Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL (13–17) Platelets 43 ×109 /L (150–400) eGFR>60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Blood cultures at admission were negative, but repeat blood cultures at the point of review 3 weeks later were positive for a mold.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fusarium solani Fusarium are species of mold that may cause disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients. It tends to be more resistant to the azole antifungals than Aspergillus species but sensitive to amphotericin. Disseminated fusariosis may be identified through positive blood cultures. The typical clinical picture is as described in a patient with prolonged (>10 days) neutropenia, persistent fevers, widespread skin lesions that evolve rapidly, and blood cultures growing a mold. Unlike aspergillosis, blood cultures are commonly positive. Mortality rates are high even with appropriate antifungals and immunotherapy such as G-CSF . Because the pathogen identified is a mold, Candida tropicalis, Histoplasma capsulatum, and Cryptococcus neoformans would not be the answer, as they appear as yeast forms in the human body. However, these pathogens can cause disseminated nodular skin lesions in immunocompromised patients. Aspergillus fumigatus is not the correct answer, as voriconazole is usually effective prophylaxis against invasive aspergillus infections, and aspergillus rarely is identified in blood cultures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q39

parts.text: Pulmonary mucormycosis - tx, risk factors, microbiology features

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: Malnutrition, patients receiving deferoxamine for iron overload, haemodialysis. Microbiology: broad ribbon like hyphae, non septate, rapid growth, thermally monomorphic, produces spores in round sporangium. Treatment: AmphoB deoxycholate, isovuconazole, posaconazole, debridement (if possible). Inherently resistant to several azoles (ketoconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole), flucytosine (5-FC) and echinocandins

questions.question: Your patient has recently undergone HSCT and presents with a lung nodule. Lung biopsy is undertaken showing the following (a Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain). [image-based question: GMS stain of lung biopsy] Please contrast Zygomycetes and Aspergillus species and complete this table (note: the table content had no relation to the photo or clinical vignette above).

parts.text: Complete the table (Organism: Zygomycetes / Aspergillus) for: Hyphae thickness; Angle of branching; Septate or aseptate

questions.model_answer: Zygomycetes (Mucorales): Hyphae thickness - broad/wide (approximately 6-25 micrometers); Angle of branching - wide-angle, typically around 90 degrees (right-angle branching); Septation - aseptate or pauciseptate (sparsely septate). Aspergillus: Hyphae thickness - narrow/thin (approximately 3-6 micrometers); Angle of branching - acute-angle, typically around 45 degrees, dichotomous branching; Septation - septate.

questions.question: Antifungal question

parts.text: What component of the cell-wall do azoles inhibit synthesis of?
Which antifungal agent is Pichia kudriavzevii (formerly Candida krusei) intrinsically resistant to?
A patient is infected with Candida auris. They have had no prior exposure to antifungal agents. What class of antifungals would you use empirically?
Name THREE antifungals active in the treatment of mucormycosis.

questions.model_answer:
a) Azoles inhibit synthesis of ergosterol, a key component of the fungal cell membrane (not the cell wall) - by blocking lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase.
b) Pichia kudriavzevii (Candida krusei) is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole.
c) For Candida auris with no prior antifungal exposure, empiric therapy with an echinocandin (e.g., micafungin or caspofungin) is recommended, given the high prevalence of fluconazole resistance in this species.
d) Antifungals active against mucormycosis: liposomal amphotericin B, posaconazole, and isavuconazole.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC guidance on Candida auris empiric treatment; general antifungal spectrum knowledge for mucormycosis.

questions.question:
Q19 (2007) Brain + Lung lesions
Man with AML getting chemo with 2 large cavitary lung lesions

parts.text: B) Voriconazole started, develops sinus necrosis. Organism?

cohort_answer.text:
A) Bacterial: S. anginosus, Anaerobic (oral flora), TB, Nocardia, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae. Fungal: Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Mucormycosis.

B) Agents of mucormycosis: Rhizopus species (47%), Mucor species (18%), Cunninghamella bertholletiae (7%), Apophysomyces elegans (5%), Lichtheimia (Absidia) species (5%), Saksenaea species (5%), Rhizomucor pusillus (4%).

C) Surgery; Ampho B; Posaconazole when improving/oral stepdown.

questions.question: AML neutropenic patient with sinusitis and necrotic palate

parts.text: What are 4 (of 10) risk factors, other than neutropenia?

cohort_answer.text: Mucormycosis - Rhizopus oryzae, Rhizomucor, Mucor, Cunninghamella (agents of mucormycosis: Rhizopus most common 47%, Mucor 18%, Cunninghamella bertholletiae 7%, Apophysomyces elegans 5%, Lichtheimia 5%, Saksenaea 5%, Rhizomucor pusillus 4%). Risk factors: Diabetes (poorly controlled, especially with DKA); Transplant (HSCT, SOT); Steroids (high dose corticosteroids); IVDU; metabolic acidosis; heme malignancy; penetrating trauma/burns; iron overload/chelation therapy with deferoxamine (no longer used). Treatment: Urgent surgical debridement; Liposomal AmB first line (5mg/kg daily) for several weeks; then step down to posaconazole or isavuconazole when improvement seen.

Zygomycetes: Rhizopus, Rhizomucor, Cunninghamella, Mucor, Lichtheimia. Treatment: L-AmB for all, +/- echinocandin for rhizopus oryzae (evidence retrospective, no evidence of superiority over amphoB monotherapy, all patients were debrided). Urgent surgical debridement; Liposomal AmB first line (5mg/kg daily) for several weeks; then step down to posaconazole or itraconazole once improvement seen.

questions.question: A guy with a skin infection that is stained and shows broad aseptate hyphae.

cohort_answer.text: Cutaneous mucormycosis. Treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B 5-10mg/kg IV q24h initially; step down to posaconazole (300mg PO BID x2 doses, then 300mg PO daily) once responding, or isavuconazole for oral step-down; duration not clearly outlined, treat until better (often prolonged). Other treatment: Surgical debridement; correction of underlying risk factors; control of hyperglycemia; reversal of ketoacidosis; rapid tapering of glucocorticoid therapy; discontinue deferoxamine if on it (not clearly shown to benefit); G-CSF if neutropenia.

questions.question: 32M with SLE on Pred + Cyclophosphamide who presents with multiple cavitary lung nodules and CNS nodules.

parts.text: List 3 pathogens that can cause this picture and treatments for each

questions.model_answer: Pathogens causing cavitary lung + CNS nodules in a heavily immunosuppressed SLE patient: (1) Nocardia species - TMP-SMX (± imipenem or linezolid for severe/CNS disease) (2) Aspergillus species - voriconazole (3) Cryptococcus neoformans - liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction, then fluconazole consolidation/maintenance.
